subChunks.title: Cross-Platform Design Tokens
subChunks.hookHtml: A design system that serves only web is half a design system. Products ship on web, iOS, Android, and sometimes desktop. When the web team defines a primary blue in Tailwind and the iOS team defines it separately in SwiftUI, two months later they are different colours. Cross-platform design tokens — a single token definition that compiles to CSS custom properties, Swift UIColor constants, Android XML colour resources, and JSON for React Native — make platform consistency a structural property of the system.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Grand Archmage Solomon: "The brand does not change when the platform changes. The token is the brand — not the CSS variable, not the Swift constant. The token. When you put the token at the centre of your system and compile to each platform's native format, consistency becomes automatic. When you don't, it becomes a full-time job."

W3C Design Token Format (DTF)

The W3C DTCG (Design Token Community Group) standard defines a platform-agnostic JSON format:

// tokens/brand.json (W3C DTF)
{
  "color": {
    "brand": {
      "primary": {
        "$type": "color",
        "$value": "{color.palette.indigo.500}",
        "$description": "Primary brand colour — used for CTAs, links, focus rings"
      }
    },
    "palette": {
      "indigo": {
        "500": {
          "$type": "color",
          "$value": "oklch(0.55 0.20 270)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Style Dictionary v4 — multi-platform compilation

// style-dictionary.config.mjs
import StyleDictionary from 'style-dictionary';

export default {
  source: ['tokens/**/*.json'],
  platforms: {
    // Web: CSS custom properties for Tailwind
    css: {
      transformGroup: 'css',
      buildPath: 'dist/web/',
      files: [{ destination: 'tokens.css', format: 'css/variables' }]
    },

    // iOS: Swift UIColor constants
    ios: {
      transformGroup: 'ios-swift',
      buildPath: 'dist/ios/',
      files: [{
        destination: 'DesignTokens.swift',
        format: 'ios-swift/class.swift',
        className: 'DesignTokens'
      }]
    },

    // Android: XML colour resources
    android: {
      transformGroup: 'android',
      buildPath: 'dist/android/',
      files: [{ destination: 'colors.xml', format: 'android/colors' }]
    },

    // React Native: JS object
    js: {
      transformGroup: 'js',
      buildPath: 'dist/react-native/',
      files: [{ destination: 'tokens.ts', format: 'javascript/module-flat' }]
    }
  }
};

Platform-specific transform groups

/* Each platform applies transforms to token values */

// CSS output: oklch colours stay as oklch
--color-brand-primary: oklch(0.55 0.20 270);

// iOS output: oklch → sRGB for UIColor
static let brandPrimary = UIColor(red: 0.318, green: 0.275, blue: 0.902, alpha: 1.0)

// Android output: oklch → hex
<color name="brand_primary">#5146E6</color>

// React Native output
export const colorBrandPrimary = '#5146e6';

Token references and aliases

/* Token references maintain relationships across outputs */
// tokens/semantic.json
{
  "color": {
    "button": {
      "background": {
        "$type": "color",
        "$value": "{color.brand.primary}",  // Reference to another token
        "$description": "Button background colour"
      }
    }
  }
}

// CSS output: resolves to CSS variable reference
--color-button-background: var(--color-brand-primary);

// iOS output: resolves to the underlying value
static let buttonBackground = DesignTokens.brandPrimary

Tailwind integration with the multi-platform output

/* globals.css */
@import "tailwindcss";
@import "./dist/web/tokens.css";  /* Style Dictionary CSS output */

/* Map generated CSS vars to Tailwind @theme */
@theme {
  --color-primary: var(--color-brand-primary);
  --color-primary-foreground: var(--color-brand-foreground);
  /* ... */
}

Solomon: "The W3C DTF format matters for the same reason any standard matters: interoperability. When Figma exports in DTF, and Style Dictionary reads DTF, and your iOS team's tools read DTF, the whole ecosystem speaks the same language. Proprietary formats create lock-in. Standards create options."

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: The token is the brand. Not the CSS variable. Not the Swift constant. The token. When you define the token once and compile to every platform, brand consistency becomes a property of your build system, not a policy you have to enforce manually.

storyBeats.speaker: One token → four platforms

subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Design a complete cross-platform token specification document from scratch. Include: the W3C DTF JSON structure for a 3-token system (primary colour, surface background, foreground text), the Style Dictionary config that compiles to CSS, iOS Swift, Android XML, and React Native TypeScript, and a comparison table showing the same token value in all four formats. No starter code.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain why cross-platform design tokens matter and what problem they solve compared to each platform team defining colours independently. Walk through how a single W3C DTF token (color.brand.primary = oklch(0.55 0.20 270)) becomes different output for each platform (CSS, Swift, Android XML, React Native) via Style Dictionary — and what the token reference syntax {color.brand.primary} means in the semantic layer.

questions.prompt: What is the W3C Design Token Community Group (DTCG) format and why does it matter?
options: A standardised JSON format for design tokens with $type, $value, and $description fields — matters because it enables interoperability between Figma, Style Dictionary, and any compliant tool
A CSS specification for declaring design tokens using @token at-rules — matters because it is natively supported by browsers
A TypeScript interface format for type-safe design tokens — matters because it enables static analysis of token usage
A Figma plugin format for exporting variables — matters because Figma is the industry standard design tool
questions.answer: A standardised JSON format for design tokens with $type, $value, and $description fields — matters because it enables interoperability between Figma, Style Dictionary, and any compliant tool
questions.explanation: The W3C DTCG format is a platform-agnostic JSON standard being developed by the Design Token Community Group. It uses $-prefixed keys ($type, $value, $description) to distinguish token metadata from structure. Its importance is interoperability: when Figma, Tokens Studio, Style Dictionary, and other tools all support the same format, tokens can flow between tools without custom transformations. It's the lingua franca of the cross-platform token ecosystem.

questions.prompt: A token value is defined as $value: {color.palette.indigo.500} using reference syntax. Style Dictionary outputs this token for CSS as var(--color-palette-indigo-500) and for iOS as a direct UIColor constant. Why the difference?
options: CSS supports cascading variable references natively, so outputReferences: true preserves the reference chain. iOS has no equivalent runtime variable system, so Style Dictionary resolves the reference to the underlying value at build time.
Style Dictionary always resolves references for web and always preserves them for native platforms
The difference is a Style Dictionary bug — all platforms should output the same reference format
CSS variables are slower at runtime, so iOS resolves to a constant for performance
questions.answer: CSS supports cascading variable references natively, so outputReferences: true preserves the reference chain. iOS has no equivalent runtime variable system, so Style Dictionary resolves the reference to the underlying value at build time.
questions.explanation: CSS custom properties are a runtime feature — the browser resolves var(--color-palette-indigo-500) when rendering. This is desirable because changing the palette value updates all semantic references automatically. iOS/Swift has no equivalent runtime variable mechanism — UIColor constants are compile-time values. Style Dictionary must resolve the entire reference chain to a concrete value at build time for the iOS output. This is why the same token produces different output formats per platform.

questions.prompt: A product ships on web (Tailwind), iOS (SwiftUI), and Android (Compose). The web team wants to use oklch colours for the design system. The iOS and Android teams warn that oklch is not natively supported in their colour systems. What is the correct solution?
options: Define primitive tokens using oklch in the W3C DTF JSON; use Style Dictionary transforms to convert oklch → sRGB hex for iOS and Android at build time; keep oklch for CSS output
Switch the entire design system to hex colours — oklch is too advanced for cross-platform use
Use oklch on web and maintain separate hex token files for iOS and Android
Tell iOS and Android teams to add oklch support — it is a CSS Color Level 4 standard and will be supported soon
questions.answer: Define primitive tokens using oklch in the W3C DTF JSON; use Style Dictionary transforms to convert oklch → sRGB hex for iOS and Android at build time; keep oklch for CSS output
questions.explanation: Style Dictionary's transform pipeline is exactly designed for this use case. The token definition is the source of truth in oklch (the most perceptually accurate colour space). Style Dictionary applies platform-specific transforms: CSS keeps oklch natively (browser support is excellent), while iOS and Android transforms convert to sRGB hex or RGB component values that their colour systems understand. This preserves the design intent in oklch while generating platform-compatible outputs automatically — no need to maintain separate token files or downgrade the entire system.
